clue.text: Harangue from one involved in commerce

indicators.note: something involved in a thing is caught up inside it, so the single letter sits within the other word

blocks.note: trade is buying and selling, commerce
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A rant delivered by somebody who works in business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One involved in commerce' reads as a trader; split it, and one is the letter being involved.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech, the same thing as a harangue.

clue.text: Army's taken over house above a stretch of water

indicators.note: in a down answer, over means placed higher, so the army's letters come first
in a down answer, above means the house's letters come before what follows

blocks.note: TA is the Territorial Army, with its 's
a manse is a minister's house
taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers have commandeered a home overlooking the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve; a manse is a Scottish or nonconformist minister's house.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tasman Sea lies between Australia and New Zealand, an example of a large stretch of water.

clue.text: Bottoms up with fine drink and a big cigar

indicators.note: turning things bottom up in a down answer inverts them, so the letters read upward

blocks.note: A1 means first-rate, written with I for 1
lager is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A drinking toast over good beer and a fat cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottoms up' looks like a toast but turns AI LAGER over to give REGALIA. A1 means excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Regalia is a dated name for a large, high-quality Cuban cigar, besides its sense of royal insignia.

clue.text: Wife gets together with doctor — an affair to which each contributes

definitions.text: an affair to which each contributes

blocks.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife
to doctor a patient is to treat them

explanation.surface: A married woman takes up with her doctor in an affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affair' suggests romance, but it is any occasion; in Cockney 'my old Dutch' (from duchess) means my wife.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch treat is an outing where every person pays their own share of the cost.

clue.text: "I'm a devotee", as procrastinator says

blocks.note: first meaning: one who worships, here speaking of themself
second meaning: what a person who puts things off says, split into three words

explanation.surface: A self-declared fan whose words are those of someone always putting things off.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as I DO LATER, the answer is exactly what a procrastinator would say; read whole, IDOLATER is the devotee.
explanation.definitionFit: An idolater worships an idol, and by extension is anyone with excessive devotion to a person or thing.

clue.text: One's ideal mate met aboard, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests one possible arrangement among many, so the letters may be reordered

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Perhaps you will find your perfect partner on a cruise ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamboat is an informal word for a very attractive person, the partner one most desires.

clue.text: Advance unaccompanied, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the word is identified by how it is said, not spelt

blocks.note: someone unaccompanied is on their own

explanation.surface: Moving forward alone, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advance' looks like a verb of movement; it is a noun for money lent.
explanation.definitionFit: An advance is money paid ahead of time and expected back, which is a loan.

clue.text: Draw man forward — put up a high ball..

indicators.note: forward means at the front, so the man's letters lead
in a down answer, put up means read upward, from bottom to top

blocks.note: Tom is a man's name; a tom is also a male
taken as written
a lob is a ball hit high in the air

explanation.surface: A game scene: a player is called forward and sends a ball up high.
explanation.walkthrough: Forward here only places the man at the front of the answer; in a down clue, put up means read from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombola is a lottery in which tickets are drawn from a turning drum, a kind of draw.

clue.text: ...after I run up — that's fraught with danger

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means read from the bottom, so the two pieces are turned round
after says the carried-over piece goes behind the letters named here

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
the dots carry over the end of 7 down, put up a high ball, which in cricket is to sky it

explanation.surface: Continuing 7 down: hitting the ball high after a run is a dangerous business.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening dots make this the second half of a sentence begun at 7 down; in cricket, to sky the ball is to hit it high in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Something risky carries the chance of harm or loss, so it is full of danger.

clue.text: Imprecation used by second-raters

indicators.note: letters used by a phrase are part of it, so the answer is found inside the words that follow

blocks.note: found running across the join of second and raters

explanation.surface: A mild curse that only inferior people would utter.
explanation.definitionFit: Drat is a mild exclamation of annoyance, and an imprecation is a curse spoken aloud.

clue.text: Shot a lot most of the time

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its last letter, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: informally, a sight means a great deal, as in a sight better
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Somebody fired off plenty of rounds for the greater part of the session.
explanation.walkthrough: ERA loses its last letter to give ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A sighter is a practice shot fired in target shooting to check the aim before scoring begins.

clue.text: Problems are recurring for humanist

indicators.note: recurring is read as running back, so the words are taken from right to left

blocks.note: sums are arithmetic problems
taken as written

explanation.surface: Troubles that keep coming back for a Renaissance scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: SUMS ARE read from the end gives ERASMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the leading Renaissance humanist scholar, a famous example of the word.

clue.text: Continually I tell them a different version

indicators.note: a different version of some words keeps their letters but puts them in another order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone complains that they keep giving people another account of events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A different version' reads as one phrase, but its A belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: All the time is an everyday phrase for constantly, without stopping, which is what continually says.

clue.text: Glass worth £25

blocks.note: first meaning: a small measure or glass of drink
second meaning: British slang for twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: A drinking vessel with a price tag of twenty-five pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: In British money slang a pony is £25 (a monkey is £500); a pony is also a small glass, as of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pony names both a small drinking measure and, in British slang, the sum of twenty-five pounds.

clue.text: Stalls as speed increases

blocks.note: tempo is the speed of a piece of music
something that increases rises

explanation.surface: An engine cuts out as it goes faster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalls' suggests an engine, but here it is a verb for playing for time.
explanation.definitionFit: To temporise is to delay a decision to gain time, which is what someone who stalls does.

clue.text: Bird or fish-eating animal

indicators.note: an animal eating something takes it inside itself, so one word swallows the other

blocks.note: a sow is a female pig
a parr is a young salmon

explanation.surface: A choice between a bird and a creature that feeds on fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish-eating animal' reads as one creature such as an otter; split it, and the animal is doing the eating of the fish. A parr is a young salmon.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparrow is a small, common brown songbird, an everyday example of a bird.

clue.text: Knotted threads we divide

indicators.note: knotted strands are twisted and tangled, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Tangled strands that we separate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divide' looks like a verb at the end of the sentence; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A watershed is the high ground dividing two river basins, and figuratively a turning point; both are a divide.

clue.text: Run the show— the heart's not in it

indicators.note: with its heart gone, a word loses its central letter

blocks.note: an opera is a staged musical show
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is in charge of the production but no longer feels any enthusiasm for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The heart's not in it' sounds like lost enthusiasm; it means the second 'the' loses its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To run a machine or business is to operate it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Ultra-late edition of paper — not a Times, it turned out

indicators.note: not a tells us one letter A is left out
the way something turned out is how it ended up arranged, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: a late extra is a special late edition of an evening newspaper
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A late-late edition that turned out not to be The Times itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultra-late' reads as one word, but the hyphen splits off the definition. A late extra was a newspaper's final special edition of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is a person holding extreme views, especially in politics, so it means an extremist.

clue.text: Pitch Prince Henry into a street

indicators.note: putting something into another thing places it inside, so the prince's letters go within the outer pair

blocks.note: A plus ST, the abbreviation for street
P is the abbreviation for prince
Hal is a pet form of Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal

explanation.surface: Throwing a member of the royal family out on to the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V. 'Pitch' looks like a verb for throwing but is the noun for tar.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitch is a black tarry substance, and asphalt is a similar bitumen mixture used for surfacing.

clue.text: Initial in signature adorned with suitable flourish

indicators.note: the initial in a word is its opening letter
the word adorned with the letter wears it, here set inside it

blocks.note: proper means suitable or fitting
the opening letter of signature

explanation.surface: Signing one's name with an elegant initial and a fitting decorative stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourish' looks like the pen-stroke of a signature; it is the verb to thrive.
explanation.definitionFit: To prosper is to thrive and do well, the same sense as the verb flourish.

clue.text: Spar with political leader in good health

indicators.note: in places the leader inside the words that follow

blocks.note: 'Good health!' is said when drinking a toast
PM is short for prime minister

explanation.surface: A politician spars with a rival while feeling fit and well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good health!' is what people say when raising a glass. 'Spar' looks like a verb for boxing; it is a ship's pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A topmast is the mast section above the lower mast on a sailing ship, one kind of spar.

clue.text: Over food a girl shows greed...

indicators.note: in a down answer, over means placed higher, so the girl's letters sit before the food

blocks.note: Ava is a girl's name
rice is a staple food

explanation.surface: A girl reveals her gluttony at the dinner table.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is extreme desire for wealth or gain, which is greed.

clue.text: Soon chapter abandons one of its members

indicators.note: whatever abandons a word leaves it, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter
a canon is a clergyman who belongs to a cathedral chapter

explanation.surface: Before long, a cathedral body will lose one of its clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: A cathedral chapter is the body of its canons, so its member is a CANON; take away C and ANON remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned word meaning shortly or in a little while, the same as soon.

clue.text: ...a girl is wrong

blocks.note: taken as written
a miss is a young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: Continuing 22 down: the greedy girl is in the wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiss means faulty or out of order, as in something is amiss, so it means wrong.

clue.text: For example, 11 rugged men are in pursuit of a forward

indicators.note: rugged ground is broken and rough, so the following letters are roughed up into a new order
what is in pursuit of something comes after it, so these letters follow

blocks.note: a prop is a forward in a rugby scrum
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Tough men chasing an attacking player, apparently on a rugby field.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to 11 across, ERASMUS, which is a proper name. PROP is a rugby forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper name, or proper noun, names one particular person or place, as Erasmus does.

clue.text: Peel some fruit noisily

indicators.note: noisily means out loud, so the word is chosen for its sound

blocks.note: a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: Loudly stripping the skin from a piece of fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To pare a fruit is to cut away its skin with a knife, so it means to peel.

clue.text: Green fabric

blocks.note: first meaning: an area of mown grass
second meaning: a fine linen or cotton cloth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Green fabric' reads as coloured cloth; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawn is a stretch of close-cut grass, like a village green, and also a fine sheer linen.

clue.text: Before 5, I am in charge

indicators.note: before places the words that follow ahead of the cross-reference

blocks.note: I am shortened, as I'm
the answer to 5 down is a dreamboat, and a lovely person is a peach

explanation.surface: Someone takes command ahead of a numbered item.
explanation.walkthrough: The number points to 5 down, DREAMBOAT, and the wordplay uses a synonym of that answer, not the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach an official is to charge them formally with misconduct, so the verbs match.

clue.text: Lawrence at home with one composer

blocks.note: T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the name Ross
someone at home is in
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Lawrence of Arabia relaxing at home in company with a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: After his Arabian adventures T. E. Lawrence joined the RAF as Aircraftman Ross.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville and William Tell, so he is an example of a composer.

clue.text: East Europeans hold the second note when backing a song

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so the note goes inside
backing means moving backwards, so the whole string is read from its end

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for East
Danes are people of Denmark
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Eastern European singers sustain a note while providing accompaniment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East Europeans' reads as one phrase; it is E plus DANES. E DANE(RE)S read backwards gives SERENADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A serenade is a song sung in the evening, traditionally by a lover beneath a window.

clue.text: An aroma is rising

blocks.note: an is the article a
a scent is a smell, an aroma

explanation.surface: A smell is drifting upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is an act of going up, so it means a rising, used as a noun.
